PET.title: Direct methods in polymer fiber diffraction – the crystal structure of poly(ethylene terephthalate)
PET.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>Using an x-ray fiber data set from poly(ethylene terephthalate) originally published in 1954, the crystal structure of the polymer was determined by direct methods, <jats:italic>via</jats:italic> symbolic addition. Of the 68 measured amplitudes, 62 were assigned phase values. Although eight of these terms were incorrectly determined, the ensuing electron density map was a sufficiently well-defined density envelope for fitting the polymer backbone, therefore directly establishing the validity of the earlier determined packing model. On the other hand, visualization of individual atomic positions in the benzene ring was not possible from the electron density map generated from this phase set, even though they would have been found if all phases had been correct.</jats:p>

PET.title: Unit cell dimensions of poly(ethylene terephthalate)
PET.authors: Stoyko Fakirov; Erhard W. Fischer; Günter F. Schmidt
PET.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>The density of crystals of poly(ethylene terephthalate), (PETP), <jats:italic>Q</jats:italic><jats:sub>c</jats:sub> is checked by X‐ray diffraction assuming a triclinic unit cell and the indices of reflections as found by <jats:italic>Bunn.</jats:italic> The following unit cell dimensions are found: <jats:italic>a</jats:italic> = 4,48Å, <jats:italic>b</jats:italic> = 5,85Å, <jats:italic>c</jats:italic> = 10,75 Å, α = 99,5°, β = 118,4°, and γ = 111,2°. This gives the density <jats:italic>Q</jats:italic><jats:sub>c</jats:sub> as 1,515g/cm<jats:sup>3</jats:sup> which is about 4% higher than that reported by <jats:italic>Bunn.</jats:italic></jats:p><jats:p>Negligible differences in spacings for samples annealed at different temperatures (120°C–260°C) have been found. Only for an annealing temperature of 100°C the higher <jats:italic>d</jats:italic>‐values lead to <jats:italic>Q</jats:italic><jats:sub>c</jats:sub> = 1,484g/cm<jats:sup>3</jats:sup>.</

Effect of Crystal Polymorphism on Elastic Modulus and Hardness of Poly(Butylene 2,6‐Naphthalate)
                    <scp>(PBN)</scp>
PBN.authors: Mengxue Du; Thomas Chudoba; Christina Wüstefeld; Ralf Lach; Katalee Jariyavidyanont; René Androsch
PBN.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The modulus of elasticity and hardness of poly(butylene 2,6‐naphthalate) (PBN) were investigated at different length scales using dynamic‐mechanical analysis (DMA), microhardness testing, and nanoindentation. By variation of the conditions of melt‐crystallization, PBN containing around 40% α‐crystals, β′‐crystals, or liquid crystals, beside glassy amorphous structure, was obtained. The absence of crystals and formation of liquid crystals, achieved by quenching the melt to ambient temperature, yield a material of relatively low stiffness and hardness of around 1/2 to 2/3 of PBN preparations containing crystals. The difference in modulus and hardness of PBN containing α‐ or β′‐crystals is minor, with slightly higher values observed for PBN composed of the amorphous glass and β′‐crystals. PBN.title: Effect of self‐seed crystal structure on growth of polymorphs in poly(butylene 2,6‐naphthalate): A cross‐nucleation study
PBN.authors: Mengxue Du; René Androsch; Dario Cavallo
PBN.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Cross‐nucleation between different crystal polymorphs is a particular, self‐seed assisted type of heterogeneous nucleation, where a fast‐growing polymorph nucleates at a pre‐existing crystal surface of another polymorph. Here, we present a study on cross‐nucleation between different crystalline phases of poly(butylene 2,6‐naphthalate) (PBN), employing hotstage polarized‐light optical microscopy and temperature‐resolved wide‐angle X‐ray scattering as analysis tools. PBN forms α‐crystals at relatively low temperature and β′‐crystals at rather high temperature, with cross‐nucleation experiments designed such to first obtain few α‐ or β′‐seed crystals (mother phase) which then are transferred to higher or lower temperature, respectively, to monitor the continuation of the crystallization process and possible growth of the other polymorph. PHB.title: Branched Polyurethanes Based on Synthetic Polyhydroxybutyrate with Tunable Structure and Properties
PHB.authors: Joanna Brzeska; Anna Maria Elert; Magda Morawska; Wanda Sikorska; Marek Kowalczuk; Maria Rutkowska
PHB.abstract: <jats:p>Branched, aliphatic polyurethanes (PURs) were synthesized and compared to linear analogues. The influence of polycaprolactonetriol and synthetic poly([R,S]-3-hydroxybutyrate) (R,S-PHB) in soft segments on structure, thermal and sorptive properties of PURs was determined. Using FTIR and Raman spectroscopies it was found that increasing the R,S-PHB amount in the structure of branched PURs reduced a tendency of urethane groups to hydrogen bonding. Melting enthalpies (on DSC thermograms) of both soft and hard segments of linear PURs were higher than branched PURs, suggesting that linear PURs were more crystalline. Oil sorption by samples of linear and branched PURs, containing only polycaprolactone chains in soft segments, was higher than in the case of samples with R,S-PHB in their structure.
